Plato, Dante, Pound & Co. Give up but Try for Rafe

Lee Harwood

Lee Harwood

Lee Harwood  

That dumb paradise

beyond the words that no one can write

from Plato down to now

“Now of the heaven which is above the heavens no earthly

poet has sung, or will ever sing in a worthy manner”.

whoever — all those “great men” —

no competition

only left with

“Let the wind speak

that is paradise”.

Agi Bene

Agi Bene

Agi Bene  

It was predictably a good, moving, learning experience, to read through Sara Rosenfeld's essays: writing which spreads over almost twenty years. This permits us to follow the main trends of Sara Rosenfeld's thinking and clinical work. We knew from the title of her essays, from Anna Freud's foreword, and from working with her in The Hampstead Clinic, that her interest and writing was centred on the “atypical” or “borderline” child's life and development. This interest started in the early fifties, when comparatively little was discussed and written about this “dark area” of childhood disturbances. It was about this time that she gathered around herself, in The Hampstead Clinic, interested child therapists and founded the Borderline Research Group. She stimulated and co-ordinated our thinking and clinical work with these “puzzling” children. The two papers which emerged from the seventeen years work in the Group were written together with the Borderline Group's secretary, Marjorie Sprince, and appeared in the Psychoanalytic Study of The Child. They are well known and often quoted, even in recent literature dealing with borderline pathology, though both papers were written in the Sixties. Sara Rosenfeld's ability to draw together, synthesise and express clearly her own and other people's findings and experiences is well reflected in these two papers. The first, “An attempt to formulate the meaning of the concept of Borderline” was an effort to define the common dynamics of these children, each of them presenting so differently from the others. The second deals mainly with the clinical and technical aspects of the treatment of the borderline child.

Reading through all the papers it struck me that it was somewhat one-sided to see Sara Rosenfeld as interested only in the atypical child, and more true to view the focal point of her interest as early development. She sought continually to evaluate and differentiate constitutional givens from early internalisations of traumatic psychic events, and to use the tool of transference to gather convincing evidence of the effects of these psychic happenings in the child. Already in her first published paper in 1953, “The changing pattern of transference in the analysis of an eleven-year-old”, she indicates how much importance she lays on the transference. The focal point of the paper here was to demonstrate that, in spite of external events and the dependence of the child on the parents, because of early and on-going internalisations, transference neurosis could develop: the analyst could become the central object of the child's libidinal and aggressive strivings. Quite a bold statement at a time when many well known American child analysts held opposite views.

Teachers of workers training for the child guidance or child psychiatric setting, of whatever discipline, need a basic text on the methods of the child psychotherapist. In many ways this book goes towards filling this gap, and it is as a presentation to the other workers of the team that this review is addressed. That is not to say that the book is not of great interest to the members of the profession of child psychotherapy, for there is much in it to read and consider. But it addresses itself to a wider field, including perhaps the general reader, and it should be judged from the wider point of view.

Firstly it must be said that although the book jacket points out that the authors whom the editors have called upon are drawn from both the Tavistock Clinic and the Hampstead Child Therapy Course and Clinic, the overall emphasis of the book is in the direction of the former. Furthermore, the relative under-representation of the orientation of the Hampstead Clinic means that the contribution of American Child Analysis towards child psychotherapy is scarcely mentioned. In particular the contributions of Eric Erikson, Bruno Bettelheim and Peter Blos, for example, go unmentioned, whilst Margaret Mahler's work on child development and child psychosis is poorly described. It is striking also that Donald Winnicott, although referred to, is not expounded upon.

This, then, is an account of child psychotherapy, its techniques, settings and theories, from the battle front, the workers in the field applying psychoanalysis to the problems coming to the clinics. The greatest strengths are the many excellent accounts of actual therapies with children and of the different settings in which the children are seen. Moreover the cases whose treatment is described are largely rather disturbed children.

Ego Strengthening Psychotherapy with Children Having Primary Ego Deficiencies11

Ivan Sherick , Charlotte Kearney , Martin Buxton and Bryan Stevens

Bryan Stevens

Ann Arbor
Michigan, 48109

Bryan Stevens  

Introduction

Child analysis is clearly the treatment of choice where the infantile neurosis is concerned (A. Freud, 1945; 1968); here interpretative work designed to alter defences, to undo repressions, etc., is called for. Exploration of fantasy material is one of the techniques used to gain insight into the dynamics of both the child and the adult patient's mental functioning. At proper moments, interpretations made in the context of the child's manifest fantasy scenarios can result in further access to unconscious conflictual material, lessen reality distortions secondary to these underlying conflicts, help to resolve conflicts and to modify pathological defenses, decrease the magnitude of neurotic symptoms, and/or provide relief from unpleasant affects such as anxiety.

In recent years in our work with children in the Day Treatment Division of the Child Analytic Study Programme, however, we have become increasingly aware of children with whom interpretative therapeutic techniques have unexpectedly resulted in a heightening of anxiety, further impairment of reality testing, and ego disorganisation. These seemingly paradoxical reactions occurred in cases which, during the outpatient evaluation and even in the early phases of treatment, appeared to be neurotic disorders amenable to traditional analytic psychotherapy. It was only after each case had progressed into treatment and after usually successful analytic techniques repeatedly resulted in little improvement or even in exacerbations of already presented difficulty that the presence of an underlying primary ego deficiency was suspected. Careful re-examination of each child's medical and psychological histories in regard to ego functions and apparatuses revealed evidence of these primary ego deficits. In several cases, the child appeared to demonstrate subtle central nervous system impairments. These were undetectable by the standard techniques for investigation of ‘organicity’, (e.g. psychological testing, neurological assessment, and eletroencephalography), and most often did not meet the criteria for being labelled “minimal brain dysfunction”, as it is most often defined (e.g. hyper-activity, severe distractibility, perseveration, motor disinhibition, etc.,). In other instances of primary ego defect, an “average expectable environment” was nonexistent, even though somatic ego apparatuses were presumably normal, i.e. there existed an average expectable endowment.

responseSet.title: An “Open Letter”
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

An “Open Letter”

James Mackeith

James Mackeith

London

James Mackeith  

In volume 4, number 3 of the Journal of Child Psychotherapy, Elizabeth Holder expressed her profound distaste for the abuse of psychiatry for political purposes in the U.S.S.R. and Eastern Europe. She argued that child psychotherapists should become involved when “… a professional discipline akin to our own and founded on the same humanistic principals is being blatantly misapplied”. She suggested that a policy of non-involvement in what psychiatrists were apparently doing in another country could be described as complicity in such circumstances.

As a result of a suggestion from a child therapist friend, I now write to draw attention to another issue. I refer to ethical problems arising from the publication of the W.H.O. Secretariat's Preliminary Review “Apartheid and Mental Health Care” — prepared for the U.N. Special Committee Against Apartheid (Published in Geneva on the 22nd March 1977). The report summarises four types of allegations about privately provided mental health care for African patients — some 8,000 to 9,000 in number.

The Institutions run by a private enterprise known as the Smith-Mitchell Company, keep in custody an exceedingly large number of Africans, admitted on an involuntary basis through a perfunctory legal and medical procedure.

The standards of care provided and the living conditions of the patients in these institutions are extremely poor and degrading, not only in comparison with the standards of a mental health care ensured for the white population, but also in relation to the most elementary and essential human needs and rights.

There is a collusion of interest between the private companies and the State, in the sense that the companies are making a profit, using Government subsidies, while the Government is spending through this arrangement less than it would have to, if mental health care for Africans were to be provided entirely by the State Services.

The chain of private institutions for mentally ill black Africans is a tool for human rights oppression and racial discrimination in the field of health care under the Apartheid system.

[[RunningHead]]

Baby and ChildPenelope Leach (London, Michael Joseph, 1977, £6.95)

N. Spyropoulos

N. Spyropoulos

London

N. Spyropoulos  

Penelope Leach has brought together her rich personal and professional experience of baby and child care in a convincing, guilt-free and sometimes humorous way. Between the commonsense lines this practical and clinical experience is expressed simply and precisely, without sounding rigidly immutable or infallible. All the essentials of an infant and child manual are painstakingly presented here, from earliest handling and everyday care of the newborn, to launching the pre-school child into life.

“Daily life with a baby or small child is made up of hundreds of minutes of minutiae. The more smoothly those minutes roll by, the more easily her hair gets washed, her meals get prepared or she is settled to sleep, the more time and emotional energy you will have for enjoying yourself and her. So no detail is too trivial to think about”.

Written from the sensible starting point of the child's immature, yet growing, awareness and understanding of herself and family, the book allows parents tremendous flexibility in approaching and coping with each child at her own level of development. Dr. Leach states very clearly how children's development during this period is constantly in forward and backstepping flux. Parents' awareness of where the child is at not only allows the opportunity of adjusting to her, but enhances their scope for fostering her progressive autonomy. What emerges concurrently with these day-to-day minutiae of caring and handling is a picture of the child's gradual physical, emotional and intellectual development, as seen in her growing individuality and interaction with those around her, and a picture of the Parents' enrichment through their interaction with her, as well as their having time to enjoy their adult relationships more.

Perhaps the most rewarding and refreshing perspective offered by her book is Dr. Leach's honest trial and error. Her fund of knowledge and feel for the child supplies us with a good number of anticipations which tend to keep the trials and errors to a minimum. This sound attitude of mind may be seen in such examples as encouraging the pre-school child to think rather than develop blind dependence and obedience, or responding to an infant's real need for comfort rather than adutomorphizing her with excessive and unrealistic expectations of the tiny infant's coping strength. Similar balance is seen in regard to the opposite extreme of infantilising the child. For Dr. Leach, “keeping a step ahead of your child” does not mean tricking, deceiving or squeezing her through a rigid mould. Instead, it means keeping a balance of what is meaningful and broadening to her, whilst at the same time allowing the Parents' love and esteem (and sanity!) for themselves and their child to grow side by side.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Fifty Years of Child Guidance

A Psychologist's View1

Doris Wills

Doris Wills

21 Maresfield Gardens
London NW3

Doris Wills  

I understand from a little book by Dr. Burbury and her co-workers (Burbury et al., 1945) that in 1920 the Tavistock Clinic was started by Dr. Crichton Miller, but that it was concerned at that time mainly with the functional disorders of adults. Not until 1927 did the Jewish Health Organisation start the first, and subsequently famous, East London Child Guidance Clinic under the direction of Dr. Emanuel Miller. At this point the Commonwealth Fund of America stepped in, and during the next year the London Child Guidance Clinic was also established, under the direction of Dr. William Moodie, who, together with certain colleagues, had the opportunity of studying the work in the United States of America. This Clinic was set up in the Canonbury district of London “after a careful study of the figures for juvenile crime in the various London areas” (Burbury et al., 1945, p. 4), and it became the main centre for the training of most of the workers practicing in the United Kingdom in the next decade or so. During this period additional clinics were established in six or seven of the major towns in England and Scotland.

Dr. Margaret Lowenfeld was another pioneer; she had established what was to become the Institute of Child Psychology in 1928, and her training course in child psychotherapy in 1933. She was a very able woman, with her own particular approach.

My first contact with child guidance was in the 1930's, when Charlotte Buhler came to England from Vienna and set up an Institute. I, and indeed several of my colleagues at the Hampstead Child Therapy Clinic, trained and worked there for some years. In spite of the fact that Charlotte Buhler denied the existence of the unconscious, she was one of the most interesting and careful observers of child development from whom it has been my good fortune to learn. Through her work, I was introduced to much that I came later to understand from another angle. For instance Charlotte Buhler described in detail what she called “work maturity”. She outlined the growth of this from the time the one-and-a-half year old begins to check himself in order to admire the two blocks he has placed one on the other, through the child's naming his building regardless of what it resembles, to the wish (at about five years) to make a realistic reproduction of a definite object. She cited a study where 80% of the children failing in the first grade in the Vienna schools proved not to have reached this stage in their play (Buhler, 1937).

In this paper I want to describe the strength of the emotions shown towards me by a ten-year-old girl from the very onset of her once-weekly treatment. The term ‘transference’ denotes the total complex of the patient's conscious and unconscious perceptions of the therapist and his feelings towards him. It has been defined many times in Psycho-analytic literature since its discovery by Freud. A good definition is that of Dina Rosenbluth (1970):

“What the child transfers and projects on to the

therapist are his unconscious images of his internal

parents or aspects of his parents, images which were

created by a fusion of his own impulses and feelings,

his own phantasies and external experience. And what

is reexperienced in the transference relationship

are the feelings, impulses and anxieties not only

from the oedipal but also from the earliest periods of life”.

Therefore facets of the transference relationship carefully observed and interpreted by the therapist are of unique importance. Winnicott writes (1958):

[[RunningHead]]

Small Children Seen and Heard in Family Therapy

Emilia Ydoiizing and Harvey Jones

Harvey Jones

Harvey Jones  

One of the reasons contributing to our interest in this topic is the pattern that seems to have evolved in family therapy which tends to avoid or too readily dismiss young children at some point during the course of family psychotherapy, almost as if they were not full members ofsuch a group. As we looked at the literature, titles such as “The Participation of Children in Family Therapy” (Ackerman 1970) or “Including the Children in Family Therapy” (Satir 1967) made us wonder who and what determined the components of the natural system, the family.

In this paper, the main aims of family therapy will be briefly examined. Next the attitudes of different clinicians to the involvement ofyoung children in the treatment will be stated. he shall then present some ideas in favour of this, and some comments as to how to make use of what, in our judgement, is the very relevant contribution of the younger members to the treatment.

Running through the paper is an implicit aim. The reader may wish to focus on the question of what sort of bridge exists between child psychotherapy and family therapy. Reference is made to information drawn from family events including child play about which the child psychotherapist has so much expertise to offer, and from which the family therapist could learn much. Perhaps reciprocally there is something to be learned about individual work with the child from there being a cross-bearing provided by data from work with the family group. Is this hoped-for interchange consonant with the challenge for inter-professional sharing made in the “Court Report”? (Committee on Child Health Services, 1976)

Aims of Family Therapy

The focus of family therapy is the family group. Symptoms presented in the individual are construed as a statement of dysfunctional relationships between members of the group of which the family is comprised. The emphasis therefore is upon a treatment approach to interpersonal relationships and not directly towards producing structural change in the individual. However, the approach implies some change of structural pattern for the group as an entity. This in turn will have profound changing consequences for those family members capable of developmental change in what is hoped will be a more favourable matrix.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Two Cases of Anorexia Nervosa 11

Cesar Botella and Sara Botella

Sara Botella

Paris

Sara Botella  

Our purpose is to bring forward certain aspects of the relationship between mother and child which can develop in hypotrophic infants born at the end of their term. We shall present a detailed observation and then make use of a second case to draw several conclusions. Only in passing do we intend to look at the structural characteristics of primary anorexia2 in infants in order to improve our understanding of the relationship between the mother and her child.

Charles

Charles is a small boy of six-and-a-half. I saw him for the first time when he was five. He impressed me with the mien of a child suffering from malnutrition: he is blond, and his blue eyes were deeply sunk in their sockets beneath chiselled temples; his veins were so apparent that his face had a bluish tinge.

The story of the child is also that of his illness, for Charles was born anorexic.

Early History and Background

Charles is the second child, following a sister one year older. Another child was born when he was two-and-a-half years old. His parents are young. There are no major conflicts between them, nor are there psychiatric antecedents.

The first meeting with Mr. and Mrs. D. was dramatic. The mother cried incessantly. Charles had been vomiting everything he ate for several months. He had got thinner. Though tall, he weighed barely twenty-six pounds.

The child had never been well, the mother said. When she was two-and-a-half months pregnant she was operated on for appendicitis. Speaking of her own vomiting during pregnancy, she later said, “I vomited him out”. The baby was born at full term and weighed five pounds one ounce. Mrs. D. felt annoyed and ashamed to have so thin an infant. This feeling remained with her throughout the years and it marked the relationship between mother and child. Though she breast fed him during the first three months, he had no appetite. He accepted very little food, and his weight hardly increased. He cried a great deal and did not sleep at night. His health was fragile. He was hospitalised for six days at the age of three months with a pulmonary infection, and again for three weeks with a recurrence at the age of nine months.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Psychotic Elements in the Neurotic Disorders of Children11

Frances Tustin

Frances Tustin

Prospect Cottage
Lee Common
Great Missenden
Bucks.

Frances Tustin  

During the past twenty five years I have practised individual psychotherapy with a wide variety of both psychotic and neurotic children. The usual distinction between psychosis and neurosis is that in psychosis awareness of commonly agreed reality is massively blocked or distorted, and in neurosis it is less so. However, in working with neurotic children I have invariably come upon a “pocket” of functioning in which awareness of reality was so blocked and distorted that it justified the term “psychotic”. What I learned from the psychotic children about the processes which blocked and distorted awareness of reality has helped me to work with these psychotic elements in neurotic children. This has seemed to increase the effectiveness of my work with such children.

I shall avoid the use of technical terms as, in so far as I can, I want to present the material from the child's point of view. I also want to make my meaning clear to those whose technical language is different from my own.

Childhood Psychosis

Of course, psychosis in children has many causes. It can be due to gross and detectible brain damage or to traumatic disturbances so early in life that it is difficult to distinguish their effects from inborn defects. These latter children may have brain damage which cannot be detected by the methods at present available, but I have found that some of them can be helped to achieve relatively normal functioning. It is from these children that the material for this paper has been drawn.

The tragedy in childhood psychosis is that due to certain pathological processes which will be discussed later, mother and child grow further and further apart in terms of a normal on-going relationship, although there is a morbid underground entanglement between them. To understand why this occurs we have to go back to the early mother-infant situation. In this early situation the nursing couple are such a unity that it is impossible to say whether the mother cuts herself off from her child or the child cuts himself off from the mother. This situation reminds one of the crossing sweeper who said, “The head's come off my broom twice already and now the handle's come off!” All that can be said with any certainty with regard to psychotic children is that the illusion of an unbroken bodily flow between mother and infant seems to have been broken in a sudden and catastrophic way and that the child experiences this as a bodily break. This brings to the infant an enraged, panic-stricken and grievous awareness of his bodily separateness from the mother.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

On Becoming A Parent11

Dinora Pines

Dinora Pines

16, Bracknell Gardens
London NW3 7EB

Dinora Pines  

Introduction

Throughout our lives we act and re-enact the role of parents and still retain within us the child we once were. The baby who puts his spoon of food to Mother's mouth is taking his first step toward parenthood, trying to feed and care for her as she had fed and cared for him. The games we play as children, “Mummies and Daddies”, “Mummy and Baby”, “Daddy and Baby”, express our feelings, our curiosity and our observations of adult life and the world about us. Thus in observing children we see the wish to have and look after a child foreshadowed early in life, both in play and fantasy, long before there is any physical possibility of parenthood. Normally a woman, usually the mother, is the first most important person in the child's life. Often little girls and boys play with dolls and soft toys, and both identify with mother as they play with the fantasy child in a quest for adult status. So maternal attitudes may be the first attributes of parenthood for both boys and girls, and the boy goes on to develop fatherliness later when he begins to admire Father's masculinity and his own, in identification with him. (Kestenberg, 1974). As the triangular situation develops between Father, Mother and Child, the child's wish fora child of his own, in identification with his parents, is expressed directly either in play or in words. The little boy wants to give mother a baby, the little girl longs to bear father's child, and primitive passions can be expressed with relative safety since the child's physical helplessness and immaturity are his best protection against the fulfilment of these early primitive drives. So little Oedipus can safely wish to murder his father and marry his mother. But since children love and need their parents too, the Oedipal Conflict is at times repressed and at other times revived throughout life, as is the wish for a child.

The First Pregnancy

It is for the first time in adolescence that a physiologically mature body enables the wish for a child to be fulfilled in reality. In pregnancy inner and outer worlds are closely linked in a woman's life. The first pregnancy in particular can be seen as a normal crisis in the search for a female identity, and the situation of the young pregnant woman and that of the earliest mother-child relationship have been vividly described by Bibring et al, (1961), Caplan (1959), Deutsch (1944), and other writers. Pregnancy is the visible proof, both to the young woman and to the world about her, that she has a sexually mature body capable of reproduction. (Erikson, 1959).

[[RunningHead]]

The Use of ‘Here and Now’ Experiences in a Teaching Conference on Psychotherapy as a Means of Gaining Insight into the Nature of the Helping Relationship

Isca Wittenberg

Isca Wittenberg

120, Belsize Lane
London NW3

Isca Wittenberg  

“If he is indeed wise, he does not bid you to enter the house of his wisdom but rather leads you to the threshold of your own mind”.

from ‘The Teacher’ by Kahlil Gibran in ‘The Prophet’.

The question of how to lead others to the threshold of their minds is one that must occupy any teacher in the art of psychotherapy and each one of us has to find his own way of setting about answering it. I have learned most at the Tavistock Clinic, where we have for many years run two basic kinds of seminars for those doing the pre-clinical psychotherapy training: Infant Observation Seminars (first introduced by Dr. Ester Bick), and Work Discussion Seminars. For the former, trainees are required to observe infants in their own homes week by week, and to make detailed reports about their observations. This heightens the student's perception of nonverbal communication and draws his attention to primitive object relationships and character development. Most people who participate in such seminars are astounded at the wealth of understanding that can be gained from attention to the minute details of infant behaviour when it is considered within the context of the infant's developing relationships, The Work Discussion Seminar for members of the “helping professions” (which Mrs. Martha Harris initiated) focuses on the student's work situation. Here the emphasis is on the relationship between client and worker, on the manifestations of transference and counter-transference. The student thus begins to look at himself in a relationship, at the reactions aroused in him by his clients and the effect of his own behaviour on the dynamics of the interaction. The seminar-leader's function in both these instances is to help the student to explore and question what is going on, to encourage him to become more aware in a feeling way of the nature of relationships. Thus, the leader starts from where the student is and enables him to think further. As therapeutic work depends so much on an individual's capacity to respond sensitively and responsibly in an always changing situation it seems particularly important not to foster any sense of dependency on the teacher, but to encourage students to think for themselves. One does not wish to impart a technique so much as to develop a student's capacity to observe, to be aware of his client's and his own feelings, and to think about emotional experiences.

[[RunningHead]]

“My Ambition is to Be Dead” The Analysis of Motives and Reasons for Suicide Behaviour in an Adolescent Girl, with Particular Reference to the Relationship between the Adolescent Process and Suicide. Parts II and III.

Part Ii: Past and Current Findings on Suicide in Adolescence1

Anne Hurry

Anne Hurry

2 1, Maresfield Gardens
London, Nb.3

Anne Hurry  

Introduction

The following attempt to compare the findings in Jessie's case with those in the literature is in no sense a complete bibliographical study. The magnitude of such a task can be seen from the thickness of Farberow's “Bibliography on Suicide and Suicide Prevention” (Farberow, 1969). For those with a particular interest in the topic, Litman's “Sigmund Freud on Suicide” (Litman, 1967) provides an excellent review of Freud's thinking on the subject, and Warren's “On Suicide” summarises much recent literature, giving some guidance through the mass of current writing. (Warren, 1976).

The emphasis in this article is on the literature since 1960 which I have found particularly useful; inevitably there will be relevant material which I have not encountered. In order to facilitate comparison with Jessie's material, I have structured this part exactly as Part I was structured, so that those wishing to refer to the clinical material relevant to any one section will find it in the correspondingly numbered section of Part I.

Background

Many writers have drawn attention to the unusually marked parental hostility frequently found in cases of adolescent suicide (Bender and Schiller, 1937; Gould, 1965; Haim, 1969; Havens, 1969; Meerloo, 1968; Schneer, 1974; Schrut, 1964; Stone, 1973). This hostility is often conscious or unusually close to consciousness, and expressed in very direct as well as subtle ways. I fully agree with Stone (1973) that “Prognostic statements about suicidal adolescents… are meaningless without inclusion of the parental factor”. In much of the literature, however, parental hostility is mentioned scarcely or not at all; Havens (1969) has expanded upon therapists’ need to deny “really” murderous wishes.

1Part 1 of this paper, the case study of Jessie, a suicidal adolescent girl, was published in the 1977 issue of this Journal.69
